title: Attentive Listening
author: Adrian Neibauer
summary: Adrian Neibauer, a fifth-grade teacher, describes how he teaches attentive listening as the foundation of a democratic, discussion-based classroom. He argues that years of notifications, games and social media have trained students to self-select what they attend to, often not the peer who is speaking. Rather than enforcing what Jeanene Turner calls entitled presence through authoritarian demands, he co-creates listening norms with students, models attentive listening himself, and borrows the First Nations Talking Stick Protocol for circle-based Family Meetings, adding listening gestures so speakers can see they are heard. His central innovation addresses a gap he noticed in seated whole-class discussion: students often did not realise a classmate was addressing the room. Drawing on the history of the typing awareness indicator, from an IBM chat-server debugging hack to Apple's three dots, and Juliana Schroeder's research on the connection those dots signal, he made laminated three-dot signs on paint sticks that students raise when they want to contribute. Early results show fewer side conversations, though some students admit they listen less while waiting to speak. He ends by situating listening as the groundwork for civil discourse and respectful disagreement.
points: Neibauer attributes students' weak peer listening to attention habits shaped by notifications, games and social media, even with phones put away.
He rejects authoritarian enforced attention in favor of co-constructed listening norms and teacher modelling, keeping a conversational rather than top-down classroom.
Listening awareness gestures, such as nods, thumbs up and sign-language style signals, give speakers visible evidence they are being heard.
His three-dot speaking indicator, modeled on messaging apps' typing awareness cue, gives seated discussions the same visible speaker signal a talking stick provides in a circle.
Initial results: fewer side conversations and more eagerness to share, though students split on engagement and some listen less while waiting for a turn.
quotes: Students are adept in self-selecting what they pay attention to and it is often not one who is speaking. Students might be eager to share their thoughts with classmates, but when it is time to listen to another peer, they disregard the speaker

Instead of the teacher having the sole authority to speak, our classroom is designed as a place where everyone in the room has something valuable to say. This means working with my students to build our classroom community and modeling how to have empathy and respect for their peers during classroom discussions. Attentive listening needs intentional practice.
Listening awareness gestures like these give the speaker observable indicators that they are being heard by the group.

A month into the school year, I have observed that when students are sitting in their assigned seats, they often do not realize that someone is addressing the class. I do not want to interrupt students mid-share to quiet down those who are still talking with their tablemates.

Since classroom discussions are not in a circle and often require time to think before responding, having a visible cue might discourage side conversations. The expectations for listening would be the same and it would be clear who is speaking.

Students are more eager to share and I have noticed a sharp decrease in side conversations and inattentiveness. The interesting thing is that when I call on someone to speak, other students are patiently holding their three-dot signs, waiting to be called on.

Teaching students how to listen to each other is the most important skill needed for a democratic, respectful classroom. Attentive listening is the foundation for all forms of group discussion like Socratic Seminars and book clubs or literature circles.
